title: Reporters on the Job: From Maine to Mexico
text:
Reporters on the Job: From Maine to Mexico
Every week, a selection of Monitor staffers and contributors share their challenges and insights from reporting around the globe.
Pownal, Maine – Karen Norris
As the Monitor’s lead designer and illustrator, I spend most of my workdays at my computer in Maine, working on a steady stream of illustrations, maps, and cover art. But this assignment was different. Pie! The pumpkin pies for our Thanksgiving issue cover had to be authentic. I donned my apron, rolled up my sleeves, and pulled out my trusty pumpkin pie recipe. The pies had to look good – but not too good. They needed that homemade charm. The next challenge: transporting these babies from Maine to our Boston headquarters. Two and a half hours of potholes and sudden braking later, I carefully delivered the pies and props for the photo shoot. Working with our photographer and layout designer, we got the “cover shot,” and then we all dug in – even our editor. Happily, the pies tasted as good as they looked. 
Topsfield, Mass. – Melanie Stetson Freeman
Some photo assignments are more fun – and more visual – than others. I knew the Giant Pumpkin Weigh-Off at the Topsfield Fair would be both. The only thing I worried about was lighting because it took place at night. As a photographer, one of the first things I think about when I walk into a space is light. Thankfully, this event was inside a brightly lit arena. I wouldn’t even have to use a flash. The setting was a dream: hilarious GIANT pumpkins, the nice people who grew them, and a friendly crowd. The only problem was that it took so long to move the enormous fruit to the scales (yes, pumpkins are fruit) that we had to stay there for five hours to find out who won.
Shelburne Falls, Mass. – Laina Gustafson
When my editors approved my pitch to cover “leaf peeping” season in New England, I couldn’t wait to see the famous foliage for myself. A charming village called Shelburne Falls was my first stop. While touring the riverside town, my guide remarked that local couples take their wedding photos in front of an ivy-covered brick wall. Every time we passed it, someone was posing for a photo. I was struck that a simple brick wall captured local culture and tourist appeal. After hours of interviews, research, and anecdotes from across New England, that ivy wall became my lede. It reminded me that while every detail matters, sometimes the heart of a story can be simple, and found in the most unassuming of places. 
Boston – Cameron Pugh
Some of the best stories sprout close to home. Or, sometimes, inside your home. That’s what happened one afternoon when I strolled into my living room and met Paul Hollings, father of my roommate, Nick. Little did I know that he is a dad in more ways than one: He grows giant pumpkins. As he described the hobby, I grew fascinated by the sheer time and dedication it took, not unlike, say, raising a son. (Mr. Hollings said, for a while, he “had to stop growing pumpkins to focus on Nicholas.”) I was sold on the story then and there, and pitched it to my editor soon after. 
Puente Caporal, Mexico – Whitney Eulich
Sometimes it takes a trail of people to lead you to a source. While reporting this week’s story about a turkey farmer in Mexico, I spoke with people across Mexico City’s restaurant and farming communities, visited two organic markets, and attended a grassroots farmers’ event. Still, I came up empty. On a hunch, I called a community center two hours away, remembering the beautifully colored chicken eggs sold there on weekends. They connected me with Carmen Quino González, whose sister raises turkeys but has no phone. Carmen generously drove to her sister’s home so we could speak by video before arranging my visit. I spent the day learning about their family and their surprisingly delicate turkeys, vulnerable to cold and scorpion bites. A little goodwill and shoe-leather reporting: a recipe for Monitor journalism.
